sharedText: hardened the hearts of the Lamanites, and blinded their minds
reason: Blinding and hardening in one clause is a KJV pairing and it belongs to John 12:40, which quotes Isaiah 6:10 — 'He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart.' Alma 48:3 has 'he had hardened the hearts of the Lamanites, and blinded their minds', with 2 Corinthians 4:4's 'blinded the minds' supplying the noun. The borrowing is real and it is adjudicated in this catalogue at Alma 10:25, with earlier occurrences at 1 Nephi 12:17 and 13:27. Within one book the formula's later appearances are the narrator's own (ADJUDICATING §4), and what is new here is only the agent: the blinder is Amalickiah rather than God or the devil.

sharedText: throwing up banks of earth round about
reason: This is the Book of Mormon's fullest description of fortification and it declines the King James Bible's vocabulary for it, which is worth recording as a negative result. The KJV's siege-work idiom is 'cast up a bank', which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 20:15, where Joab casts up a bank against Abel of Bethmaachah; the cognate 'cast a bank against it' stands in two more, 2 Kings 19:32 and Isaiah 37:33, both of Sennacherib. Alma 48:8 has 'throwing up banks of earth round about, to enclose his armies, and also building walls of stone to encircle them about' — a different verb, an added material, and, decisively, the opposite military function: the KJV's bank is always thrown up by a besieger against a city, and Moroni's is thrown up around his own men. Shared noun, opposed engineering.

The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate. Amos 3:11 — 'An adversary there shall be even round about the land; and he shall bring down thy strength from thee' — and Alma 48:9's 'yea, all round about the land … and thus he did fortify and strengthen the land'. Four words of pure spatial connective, and the two texts pull in opposite directions: Amos surrounds a land with an enemy, Alma surrounds it with fortifications. The verbal coincidence of an adversary and a strength brought down is close enough to tempt, which is why it is entered rather than passed over.

The machine proposes Jehoshaphat's assembly — 'all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children' — for Alma 48:10's list of what Moroni was preparing to defend: 'their liberty, their lands, their wives, and their children, and their peace'. It is a real resemblance and the wrong verse. The list is the same one written on the title of liberty at Alma 46:12, where it is adjudicated against Nehemiah 4:14, the KJV's one muster speech built out of exactly this catalogue of dependents; the recurrence is recorded on that link. 2 Chronicles 20:13's list has the little ones the Book of Mormon's does not, lacks the possessions the Book of Mormon's does have, and belongs to a prayer meeting rather than a mobilization.

sharedText: the very powers of hell would have been shaken
reason: 'If all men had been, and were, and ever would be, like unto Moroni, behold, the very powers of hell would have been shaken forever' states as a counterfactual what Matthew 16:18 states as a promise — that hell will not prevail against a body of the faithful — and it is the most quoted sentence in the chapter, so its absence from the link register needs explaining. 'Gates of hell' is a KJV singleton; 'powers of hell' occurs in no KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon's verb is 'shaken' where Matthew's is 'prevail'. The one shared noun is unavoidable in any sentence about hell. Matthew 16:18 is adjudicated in this catalogue at 2 Nephi 4:32 and carried as a composite at Mosiah 26:15, where the wording actually points; here the resemblance is at the level of the idea and the idea is common property.

'They were highly favored of the Lord' uses a KJV singleton — 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured' — which enters the Book of Mormon in its first verse (1 Nephi 1:1) and thereafter functions as a standing formula. It is adjudicated within Alma at 13:23, with the Mosiah instance at 1:13. A fresh row here would be the narrator's own idiom, not a new dependence.

'Sending so many of their brethren out of this world into an eternal world, unprepared to meet their God' turns on 'prepare to meet thy God', which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Amos 4:12. The catalogue adjudicates it at Alma 5:28, with recurrences at 5:29 and 5:31, where Alma's sermon uses it as its refrain and the argument can be made in full. Its appearance here as a soldier's scruple about killing the unrepentant is a striking application, and it is a use of Alma's phrase rather than a fresh borrowing from Amos.

sharedText: if they should keep his commandments, they should prosper in the land
reason: The chapter closes on the Book of Mormon's covenant formula, quoted as 'the promise of the Lord' — the 1830 reads 'the promise of the Lord were', which 1920 corrected to 'was'. Its Deuteronomic background (Deuteronomy 29:9, 30:16, Joshua 1:7-8) supplies no sentence and its conjunction is not the KJV's; the formula is adjudicated at its first use rather than on each of its several hundred repetitions, and the register's entry at Alma 36:1 sets out the reasoning. Entered here so a reader of Alma 48:25 is not left supposing the catalogue overlooked the verse it ends on.
